item.title: SeatGeek Canada hit with more fines totalling $22,500 over ticket resale violations
item.description: SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value. The province’s consumer beware website shows the new fines issued to the ticket resale platform earlier this month total $22,500 collectively. The website says the first of the two fines amounts to $15,000 and is for allegedly making a ticket available for sale or facilitating a sale of a seat beyond the resale price limit. The second fine is for $7,500 and is for allegedly failing to disclose the total price of a ticket when a seat was purchased from a primary seller. SeatGeek Canada did not answer questions about what events the fines stem from or whether it will fight the penalties. “We are doing our best to comply but we have yet to receive meaningful direction from the government on how to do so,” spokesperson Cameron Papp said Thursday in an email. Giulia Paikin, a spokesperson for the Ontario Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery Stephen Crawford, also did not answer questions about the nature of the penalties. However, she sent a statement that repeated nearly verbatim what the province has previously said about anyone responsible for price cap violations facing fines of up to $250,000. “We will not hesitate to hold bad actors who break the rules accountable,” an email from Paikin said. SeatGeek’s new fines stem from legislation the province implemented earlier this year, after fans complained about resale prices for tickets to Taylor Swift’s Eras tour in 2024 and last year’s playoff run by the Toronto Blue Jays. The legislation was meant to keep people from reselling seats to Ontario events for well beyond face value and tamp down on scalpers profiting off their ability to scoop up tickets to hot concerts and shows. After the legislation came into effect, the province issued $25,000 in fines to SeatGeek in August for similar offences. A $20,000 fine for fellow resale website StubHub Canada followed in September. When SeatGeek was given its first round of fines, it told The Canadian Press it had notified third-party sellers on its platform about the new law but was still seeking guidance from the province around how to comply with the regulations. The platform argued it is challenging to confirm the original value of tickets because many sellers don’t have access to that information. Sometimes seats have changed hands several times before they wind up on a resale site and if tickets were bought as part of a broader package, like a season’s seat arrangement, it can be hard to break down the value of a single ticket. To address these issues, SeatGeek said it has asked Ontario to define what counts as acceptable proof of a ticket’s original price and for guidance around how a marketplace is expected to validate the cost of seats. --- Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

item.title: Nova Scotia premier defends changing his stance on welcoming data centre proposals
item.description: Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is defending his decision to change his stance on when data centres might be considered for approval to operate in the province.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: HALIFAX — Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is defending his decision to change his stance on when data centres might be considered for approval to operate in the province. In June, the premier said it was too soon to turn his government’s attention to the matter, and that it would not be discussed until far into the future. A few months later, he softened that stance, opening a door to consider proposals from the sector. “A lot has happened … in the world, geopolitics, all kinds of situations there,” Houston told reporters Thursday. “When you look at some of the positioning of the federal government around data sovereignty, around the regulations that would be required, (they) definitely were thoughtful and had an impact on me.” The premier had previously said discussions about data centres would have to wait until the province had completed major energy generation projects, including the ambitious Wind West offshore wind farms. “We’re going to generate significant amounts of energy … (and) at that point in time, that would be a more appropriate discussion,” he said on June 18. At the time, the premier said the discussion about data centres “is so far out in the future … but there wouldn’t be a commitment to a data centre unless we could fully supply the energy without any risk to Nova Scotians.” Late last month, however, Houston said data centres are becoming increasingly critical pieces of infrastructure, adding that Canada can’t rely on other countries to store its data. He said he became more open to considering data centre proposals after Ottawa rolled out its new rules. “I think the sentiment of that (June) statement was that we wouldn’t allow an impact on ratepayers,” Houston said Thursday. “We’re not going to drive up the rates to let another user, any type of industrial use, have their power while households and Nova Scotians pay more. That sentiment remains.” Data centres, used in AI and other high-tech industries, are typically massive operations that require immense amounts of electricity to run and cool off computer servers. EverWind Fuels, the company planning a large-scale green hydrogen project in Cape Breton to be powered by onshore wind, says it’s exploring setting up a data centre at an existing industrial site at Point Tupper, N.S. The proposed data centre “would form part of the broader Point Tupper Energy Hub and complement EverWind’s clean energy projects across Nova Scotia,” company spokesperson Claire Parsons said in an email Thursday. Parsons declined to say if the proposed data centre would be used for artificial intelligence. Official Opposition Leader Claudia Chender called Houston’s changed stance on data centres a “stunning reversal.” “When the premier said not long ago that we were not considering AI data centres, not today, not tomorrow … people took him at his word as they watched these debates play out in other places,” Chender, the NDP leader, told reporters Thursday. Last month, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew rejected plans for a massive AI data centre southeast of Winnipeg. Kinew said the project’s size, energy use and community impact outweighed its limited gains. He said he was also skeptical of the long-term demand for centres of this scale given advances in computing. Meanwhile, Bell Canada intends to quadruple the size of its planned data centre project in Saskatchewan, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying last month the project is expected to bring in more than $50 billion in capital investment. Alberta has also embraced data centre development. Electricity generator TransAlta Corp. announced plans in February to power a new data centre west of Edmonton. This came after the provincial technology minister said in 2024 that province was hoping to see $100 billion worth of artificial intelligence data centres under construction over five years. Environmental advocates have raised concerns about the massive volume of energy and water used by data centres. They’ve also warned about the potential for chemical pollution. A recent United Nations University report says the environmental footprint of data centres globally already rivals some of the world’s largest countries. The report also predicts their water and energy use and pollution will double in just four years as use of artificial intelligence grows. Chender and interim Liberal leader Iain Rankin both said Thursday they have serious concerns about the potential environmental impacts and water use tied to a data centre. Houston said Thursday a data centre in Nova Scotia would have to go through an approval process that could exceed federal requirements. This means the process would need to consider the impact on the environment and ratepayers. Both opposition leaders said these protections should be built into legislation. “It’s one thing to say that water and environmental concerns and ratepayers will be protected, but it’s not a fact that the premier’s word is stronger than regulations or legislation,” Rankin said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026. Lyndsay Armstrong, The Canadian Press

item.title: Wall Street muscles higher despite more swings for AI stocks
item.description: A sell-off for artificial-intelligence stocks is hitting Wall Street again Thursday after whipping around the world on worries about how much longer the AI frenzy will last.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — U.S. stock indexes muscled higher Thursday, led by companies delivering bigger profits. They pulled closer to their records even as stocks in the artificial intelligence industry kept swinging on worries about how much longer their boom will last. The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent after erasing an early-morning loss and pulled closer to its all-time high set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 556 points, or 1.1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite added 0.1 per cent. Marsh & McLennan helped lead the way and rallied 4.6 per cent after the insurance and professional services firm that updated its brand name to Marsh reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Expectations are high for growth in profits from all kinds of companies this reporting season, which began in earnest this week. That’s what’s allowed U.S. stocks to set records despite high inflation and the many other worries weighing on Wall Street. Kimberly-Clark climbed 4.7 per cent after the company behind Huggies, Kleenex and Kotex said it expects to report revenue and profit for the latest quarter above what analysts had been expecting. Bank of New York Mellon rose 3.2 per cent after reporting a stronger profit than analysts expected, and CEO Robin Vince said BNY saw strength across its regions. Markets had been much shakier earlier in the day. A sell-off for AI stocks that began on Wall Street Wednesday whipped around the world and sent South Korea’s Kospi stock index down 7.6 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 down 4.9 per cent before knocking the S&P 500 lower at the start of Thursday’s trading. They’re the latest jarring moves for AI stocks after they led the market for years. Companies are pouring money into the technology in hopes of bigger profits and improved productivity. But data centers and AI chips cost money, and many companies have been borrowing the cash to get them. Now, after yields in bond markets worldwide hit their highest levels in years and made borrowing money more expensive, worries are rising about how resilient that boom in spending can be. High yields in the bond market also generally make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks, particularly those seen as the most expensive. Nvidia, the chip company that’s ridden the AI boom to become Wall Street’s most valuable company, fell 1.8 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It came into the day with a nearly 1,415 per cent gain since the end of 2022. But the losses for AI stocks moderated as the day progressed, which helped broad U.S. indexes to steady. Nvidia more than halved an early-morning loss that had reached 3.8 per cent. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. ’s stock that trades in the United States dropped as much as 5.3 per cent in the morning before finishing with a more modest loss of 1.8 per cent. The bellwether for the AI industry reported a profit for the latest quarter that topped analysts’ high expectations, and Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang said it expects strong demand to continue in the final three months of 2026. CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, fell as much as 9.5 per cent in the morning after tumbling 15.5 per cent a day earlier. It later flipped to a gain and finished 5.9 per cent higher. All told, the S&P 500 rose 25.12 points to 7,744.06. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 556.21 to 52,177.69, and the Nasdaq composite added 20.16 to 26,713.03. In the bond market, Treasury yields fell, which means investors were willing to pay higher prices to buy U.S. government bonds. Treasurys have a reputation as a safer investment, and investors often flock to them when feeling nervous. The yield on the 10-year Treasury sank to 5.09 per cent from 5.19 per cent late Wednesday. It had topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors. The drop in yields came even though another report signaled inflation has worsened in the United States by more than economists expected. Several reports on the U.S. economy also came in stronger than economists expected, which typically pushes yields upward. One report said U.S. retailers made more money last month than economists expected, while another said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week than expected. In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s loss was the headliner. Its Kospi index is dominated by two chip companies, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, and it fell to its worst day since July. It has dropped 39 per cent since setting a record in June. Indexes were stronger in Europe, which has less of a dependence on tech stocks. London’s FTSE 100 rallied 1.1 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writers Chan Ho-him and Matt Ott contributed to this report.
